questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
a high academic level at the university
the university had an international outlook (e.g. embraced and included international students)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: was connected to a member of staff at the university (who e.g. did an introduction for the new students in his group)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Got housing through the university's student accommodation which I got quite easily and quickly – but do this as early as possible as you are not guaranteed a space and they may be filled quickly. Also be aware that you most likely will not get one of the places you asked for (I ended up getting one not on my list of choices)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: You will most likely live with roommates – talk to them about sharing the cost of e.g. pots and pans, toilet paper etc. It will save you money in the long run

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You could pick up to 10 courses from their couse catalogue and sent them in to the university ranked(check the prerequisites!). You then got put into three (or the amount needed to make a total of 30 ECTS) and when the semester started there was a two week period where you could request courses changes if needed

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A course catalogue with descriptions and time tables of all the available courses + an email you could write to if one needed help (I didn't use this)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Mostly successful – there were two courses that I would have liked more to have gotten into but they were filled when I requested a change. Overall, I ended up being very happy with the courses I had though

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Keep your expectations low – but if there is a course you really won't you might have to be insistent on e.g. sending in requests for a course change; there are changes all the time over the two week period

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I ended up having to take 1st- and 2nd-year courses only (I'm studying Danish so my pre-requisites to courses were limited and therefore limited the number of courses available to me) but generally I found the level lower than I'm used to. At the same time, I found that you could easily self-adjust the level e.g. through recommended extra reading and the teachers were very open to giving you extra material etc.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The number of hours in a week was about the same but was (instead of two- or three hours long) all limited to 50 minutes of teaching and therefore more spread out throughout the week, e.g having two lectures of one hour each on two different days, instead of one two hour lecture.
Also, I had so-called 'tutorials' where a small group of students (8-10) sat down with a teacher each week to discuss the week's reading and topic. This was very rewarding

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Morality and Value
Scottish Literature 2A
Migration, Diaspora, exile: the politics of representation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: if you are a humanities student, take a course at the Scottish Studies Institute (e.g. Scottish literature or Scottish studies)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you want to join a university sports team (or other students' associations), this will easily become very expensive (often you will need a gym membership in addition to the cost to the association itself)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I spent very little money on course books/materials as almost all them were available online

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All sorts (I don't have the overview) – but I was personally part of the Badminton club with weekly training

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: A sports team is fun – also lots of the associations arrange events open to all students throughout the semester

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: explore the many nature areas near the city – also, the Highlands are beautiful but can be harder to get to (there are lots of tours though, e.g. through the Erasmus Student Organization)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It is a very international university and city in general so it is easy to meet other international students for example but harder to find and meet 'true Scots' – also, I found it quite difficult to connect to other students outside of my courses (e.g. no Friday-bars as I'm used to back home)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing was particularly hard but I did have to practice saying 'please' and 'thank you' much more often than I'm used to

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed the pub culture and how willing students were to talk in both the lectures and in classes in general

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
It might seem like everyone is having the most fun all the time (going out, making so many new friends etc.) but remember to listen to yourself and rest when you need to; a night in with your roommates can be just as fun and memorable as a night out
Be open to talking to anyone and don't be afraid to strike up a conversation; there are so many interesting and different people in the world
Try to be realistic about what's possible: there are so many possibilities available to you and it's impossible to do everything, try to find a balance between socialising and studying, striking up new friendships and calling your friends back home (I know it's hard to don't beat yourself up if it doesn't succeed all the times)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: it's impossible to do all the things available to you so try to pick a couple of the ones you find the most interesting (e.g. a student organization) and cultivate these

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: you get to really push yourself and your boundaries and I found a whole new level of independence and here through self-confidence

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
while life living abroad can be really intense and full of new people and new experiences, it can also be quite lonely and I felt at times cut off from my friends and family back home; it can be challenging trying to both establish new relations and keeping up with you loved ones back home
Having people visit is really nice but can also be time-consuming and make you miss home so much more so try to find a balance that fit your needs

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
